title: Data Science I with python
text:
Preface
Welcome to STAT 303-1 (Data Science with Python I), Section 20 at Northwestern University.
This book combines foundational concepts with hands-on practice. Its overall organization was adapted from earlier course materials developed by Professor Arvind Krishna. The chapters, examples, assignments, and technical guidance have since been revised and expanded for the current course.
In this first course, you will:

Learn to use essential Python libraries for data science, including but not limited to NumPy, Pandas, and Matplotlib. These three are the main focus, but you will also be introduced to other useful libraries and tools as needed for real-world data analysis.
Develop skills in Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), transforming messy, real-world datasets into meaningful insights through visualization, summarization, and pattern discovery

The book is organized to guide you step-by-step:

Review of STAT 201: Python Foundations: Review Python basics and data structures from STAT 201 in two unnumbered chapters. You can use your existing STAT 201 setup for this review. For additional practice, visit the STAT 201 ebook.
Setting Up for Data Science (Chapters 1–2): Work in Jupyter notebooks inside VS Code, refresh the Quarto HTML submission workflow, and manage project environments and local data paths. Each chapter ends with a practice activity; Assignment B applies the complete workflow in a new project.
Core Library Foundations (beginning with Chapter 3, Reading Data): Extend your Python programming skills with essential third-party libraries for data science.
From Messy to Insight: Prepare, combine, and explore data to answer meaningful questions.
Assignments A–G: Begin with Assignment A for prerequisite Python practice, then Assignment B for project setup, followed by Pandas, NumPy, visualization, cleaning, and wrangling. See Canvas for due dates.
Appendix H — Geospatial Plotting: optional reference for final projects that involve locations. It is not assigned and has no activity; read it when a project calls for a map.

Throughout the quarter, this resource will be updated and refined to improve clarity, depth, and alignment with our teaching objectives.
As a living document, your feedback and suggestions are always welcome. Contributions from students, instructors, and the broader academic community help make this book stronger and more effective.
If you have ideas for improving the textbook, please share your feedback or suggestions using our dedicated Textbook Improvement Form. Your input is invaluable in making this resource better for everyone.
Thank you for joining us on this learning adventure. We hope this book becomes a valuable companion as you build your skills and confidence in data science with Python.

This chapter reviews the Python programming foundations from STAT 201 that you will use in STAT 303-1. Use your existing STAT 201 Python setup: the executable examples need only Python and its standard library. No data science packages are required yet.
Begin with the diagnostic. If you can explain your answers, skim the corresponding sections; otherwise, work through the examples and checks. For a fuller explanation of prerequisite material, return to the STAT 201 book.
By the end of this review, you should be able to trace assignments, choose conditions and loops, write functions that return reusable results, import a standard-library module, distinguish attributes from methods, and interpret common error messages.

title: Python Basics
text:
Variables, Types, and Expressions
A variable name refers to an object. Assignment binds a name to an object; later assignment can bind the same name to a different object, even one of a different type.
Use descriptive snake_case names such as temperature_c and valid_count. Names are case-sensitive, cannot start with a digit, and cannot be reserved keywords such as for. Letters, digits, and underscores cover the names we will use; Python also permits many Unicode letters. Avoid hiding built-ins with names such as list, str, or sum.

temperature_c = 18.5
station_count = 3
is_valid = True
station_name = "North"
missing_reading = None

for value in [temperature_c, station_count, is_valid, station_name, missing_reading]:
    print(repr(value), type(value).__name__)

18.5 float
3 int
True bool
'North' str
None NoneType


Here, int, float, bool, and str are types; None is a special value whose type is NoneType. It commonly represents the absence of a value. A numeric zero can be a valid measurement and should not automatically be treated as missing.
Lists, tuples, sets, and dictionaries organize collections of values. Strings are immutable text sequences. We will review these structures in the next chapter.

Convert deliberately
Text that looks numeric is still text. float() and int() convert suitable values; str() creates a text representation. Conversion can fail when the content does not match the requested type.

reading_text = "18.5"
reading_value = float(reading_text)
print(reading_value + 2)
print(reading_text + "2")

20.5
18.52


The first operation adds numbers; the second joins strings. float("unknown") would raise ValueError. Likewise, int("18.5") fails: that text is not an integer literal. Decide what a value means before converting it.


Operators and assignment



Expression
Meaning




a + b, a - b, a * b
Addition, subtraction, multiplication


a / b
Division


a // b, a % b
Floor division and remainder


a ** b
Exponentiation


a == b, a != b
Equality and inequality


a < b, a <= b, a > b, a >= b
Ordered comparisons



= assigns a value; == compares values. Use parentheses to make a calculation’s intended order clear.

temperature_c = 20
temperature_f = temperature_c * 9 / 5 + 32
print(f"{temperature_c} degrees C = {temperature_f} degrees F")

lower_limit, upper_limit = 0, 100
print(lower_limit, upper_limit)

20 degrees C = 68.0 degrees F
0 100


An f-string inserts values into text using {...}. The last assignment unpacks two values into two names. Ordinary unpacking requires matching counts; starred unpacking is reviewed in Data Structures.
Check: Set reading_text = "12.5". Convert it to a number, add 0.5, and display Adjusted reading: 13.0.






NoteOne solution





reading_text = "12.5"
adjusted_reading = float(reading_text) + 0.5
print(f"Adjusted reading: {adjusted_reading}")

title: Python Basics
text:
Conditions and Logic
A condition determines which code runs. Indent the body consistently with four spaces. Configure your editor to insert spaces when you press Tab; mixing tabs and spaces can cause errors.

reading = 105

if reading is None:
    status = "missing"
elif 0 <= reading <= 100:
    status = "within the expected range"
else:
    status = "needs investigation"

print(status)

needs investigation


Python checks branches in order and runs the first matching branch. The else branch runs if none match. The range here is an example rule, not a universal definition of valid data: a real analysis needs a rule appropriate to the measurement.
Use is None to check for the special missing-value placeholder. Use == to compare ordinary values. Checking for None first avoids trying to compare it with a number.

Combine conditions

and: both conditions must hold.
or: at least one condition must hold.
not: reverses a truth value.

Python short-circuits and and or: it evaluates the second expression only when needed.

reading = None
is_acceptable = reading is not None and 0 <= reading <= 100
print(is_acceptable)

reading = 105
outside_range = reading < 0 or reading > 100
print(outside_range)
print(not outside_range)

False
True
False




Truth values are not data-quality rules
Common false values include False, None, numeric zeros, and empty strings and collections. Other objects can define their own truth behavior; this is not an exhaustive list. bool() is a built-in function for checking truth values.

print(bool(0))
print(bool(None))
print(bool(""))
print(bool("0"))

False
False
False
True


"0" is nonempty text, so it is true. For numerical measurements, if reading: cannot distinguish a valid zero from None. Use an explicit check that matches your question. Later, arrays and tables will require their own tools for combining conditions and checking missing data.
Predict → run → explain: Change reading in the first branching example to None, 0, and 101. Which branch runs each time? Why would if not reading: be unsuitable for detecting only missing readings?






NoteCheck your reasoning





None is missing, 0 is within the expected range, and 101 needs investigation. Both None and 0 are false in a truth test, so if not reading: groups together two different situations.

title: Python Basics
text:
Loops and Iteration

Start with a for loop
A for loop visits each item in an iterable, such as a list, string, or range. You do not need a counter just to access each item.

readings = [18.5, None, 21.0, -2.0, 0.0]
valid_count = 0
valid_total = 0.0

for reading in readings:
    if reading is not None and 0 <= reading <= 100:
        valid_count += 1
        valid_total += reading

print(f"Valid readings: {valid_count}")
print(f"Total: {valid_total}")
if valid_count > 0:
    print(f"Mean: {valid_total / valid_count:.2f}")

Valid readings: 3
Total: 39.5
Mean: 13.17


The loop includes the valid zero. It excludes missing and out-of-range readings using an explicit rule. Checking the count before division handles the possibility of no valid readings.
Modify: Replace readings with [None, -2.0]. What should the program report? What happens if the guard before division is removed?






NoteExpected result





The count is 0 and the total is 0.0; no mean is printed. Without the guard, division by zero raises ZeroDivisionError. For a report, you could add an else branch displaying "No valid readings".





Use range() when you need integer steps
The stop value is always excluded. A positive step moves upward; a negative step moves downward. If the direction cannot reach any value before the stopping boundary, the range is empty. A step of zero is invalid.

print(list(range(4)))
print(list(range(1, 4)))
print(list(range(1, 8, 2)))
print(list(range(3, 0, -1)))

[0, 1, 2, 3]
[1, 2, 3]
[1, 3, 5, 7]
[3, 2, 1]


For an item and its position, enumerate() is usually clearer than indexing through range(len(...)). Data Structures reviews that pattern in more detail.


break and continue
break exits the nearest enclosing loop. continue skips the remaining statements in the current iteration and starts the next iteration.

# Stop at the first reading that needs investigation.
for reading in [18.5, 105.0, 21.0]:
    if reading > 100:
        print(f"Investigate: {reading}")
        break
    print(f"Checked: {reading}")

Checked: 18.5
Investigate: 105.0



# Skip missing entries while keeping valid zeros.
for reading in [18.5, None, 0.0]:
    if reading is None:
        continue
    print(f"Recorded: {reading}")

Recorded: 18.5
Recorded: 0.0


Predict: Why is 21.0 not checked in the first example? Why is 0.0 printed in the second?






NoteExplanation





break ends the first loop when 105.0 is encountered. In the second loop, only None triggers continue; zero remains a valid entry.





Use a while loop for a stopping condition
A while loop repeats while its condition is true. Identify what changes on each iteration and why the loop will eventually stop.

# Compute 10! = 1 * 2 * ... * 10.
n = 10
factorial = 1
factor = 1

while factor <= n:
    factorial *= factor
    factor += 1

print(f"{n}! = {factorial}")

10! = 3628800




Diagnose an infinite loop without running it
The following example is displayed for inspection, not included as an executable notebook cell. Do not paste it into a running cell unchanged.
factor = 1
while factor <= 10:
    print(factor)
    # The value of factor never changes.
Repair it: Which line belongs inside the loop? If a loop runs unexpectedly, interrupt execution using your notebook’s stop/interrupt control, then inspect the condition and update before running it again.






NoteRepair





Add factor += 1 inside the loop. The condition eventually becomes false when factor reaches 11. A condition such as while factor > 0 would still not stop when repeatedly increasing a positive factor.

title: Python Basics
text:
Functions and Return Values
A function gives a reusable operation a name. It can accept zero or more arguments. Defining a function does not run its body; calling it does.

return versus print
print() displays information. return sends a value back to the caller so another calculation can use it. A function that reaches its end without returning a value returns None.

def show_fahrenheit(celsius):
    print(celsius * 9 / 5 + 32)

shown_result = show_fahrenheit(20)
print(f"Stored result: {shown_result}")

68.0
Stored result: None



def celsius_to_fahrenheit(celsius):
    """Return a Celsius temperature converted to Fahrenheit."""
    return celsius * 9 / 5 + 32

converted = celsius_to_fahrenheit(20)
print(f"Converted: {converted}")
print(f"Five degrees higher: {converted + 5}")

Converted: 68.0
Five degrees higher: 73.0




Parameters, keyword arguments, and defaults
A parameter is a name in a function definition. An argument is a value supplied in a call. Arguments may be supplied by position or by keyword. A parameter with a default may be omitted from the call.

def is_valid_reading(value, lower=0, upper=100):
    """Return whether a numeric reading is present and within the limits."""
    return value is not None and lower <= value <= upper

print(is_valid_reading(18.5))
print(is_valid_reading(None))
print(is_valid_reading(105, upper=120))
print(is_valid_reading(value=-2, lower=-10, upper=40))

True
False
True
True


This function expects a number or None; it does not convert arbitrary text. Documenting that expectation helps the caller use it correctly. Keyword arguments make choices such as upper=120 visible at the call site.
Write: Define adjust_reading(value, offset=0) to return value + offset. Call it once with the default and once using a keyword argument.






NoteOne solution





def adjust_reading(value, offset=0):
    return value + offset

print(adjust_reading(18.5))              # 18.5
print(adjust_reading(18.5, offset=0.5))  # 19.0





Local names and global names
Parameters and names assigned inside a function are normally local to that function. A function can read names from its module’s global scope, but passing required values as arguments makes dependencies easier to see.

station_label = "North"  # Global name in this notebook.

def display_station():
    print(station_label)  # Reads the global name; does not declare a local one.

def make_station_label(name):
    cleaned_label = name.strip().title()  # Local name.
    return cleaned_label

display_station()
print(make_station_label("  south  "))

North
South


cleaned_label is not made available outside make_station_label; its value is made available through return. Assignment to a name inside a function normally creates or updates a local binding rather than rebinding a global name. Shared mutable objects are a separate issue, reviewed in Data Structures.






NoteOptional review: flexible argument lists





In documentation, *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple and **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary. The * and ** syntax gives these names their roles; the names themselves are conventions.
def describe_call(*args, **kwargs):
    print(args)
    print(kwargs)

describe_call(18.5, 21.0, unit="C")
# (18.5, 21.0)
# {'unit': 'C'}
For this review, prioritize ordinary parameters, returned values, and keyword arguments. You do not need to design flexible interfaces before starting STAT 303-1.

title: Python Basics
text:
Built-ins and Imports








Tool
Where it comes from
How you use it




len, sum, type, print
Built into Python
Call directly


math, datetime, statistics
Python standard library
Import; no separate package installation


NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib, Seaborn
Third-party packages
Install in a project environment, then import



An import makes a module or selected names available to your program; it does not install a package.

import math
from statistics import mean
import datetime as dt

print(math.sqrt(81))
print(mean([18.5, 21.0, 0.0]))
observed_at = dt.datetime(2025, 9, 20, 11, 30)
print(observed_at.strftime("%b %d, %Y"))

9.0
13.166666666666666
Sep 20, 2025


import math imports a module, from statistics import mean imports a particular name, and import datetime as dt gives a module an alias. %b is the abbreviated month name in the current locale, so its displayed language can vary.
We will install third-party packages after the review, in Project Environments, Packages, and File Paths. Different projects can need different packages and versions; that motivates keeping their environments separate.

title: Python Basics
text:
Objects, Attributes, and Methods
Names refer to objects. An object’s attributes are accessed using a dot; its methods are operations associated with the object. A method is itself an attribute that you can call.

observed_at = dt.datetime(2025, 9, 20, 11, 30)
print(observed_at.year)                    # Read an attribute.
print(observed_at.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"))    # Call a method.

station_label = "north"
print(station_label.upper())
print(station_label)                      # Strings are immutable.

2025
2025-09-20
NORTH
north


Parentheses call the method. station_label.upper() returns a new string; it does not change the existing string. Later, library objects will also expose attributes and methods. Learn to check what an operation returns and whether it changes its object.
Explain: Why does observed_at.year() raise TypeError?






NoteExplanation





observed_at.year is an integer attribute, not a callable method. Retrieve its value without parentheses. The error says that an int object is not callable.

title: Python Basics
text:
Understanding Python Errors
Read the error type and message, then locate the indicated line in your code. Use the surrounding values and types to explain the cause before changing anything.
The following examples are shown as text so that running all executable cells does not intentionally fail.








Example
Error
What to investigate




print(undefined_reading)
NameError
Has that name been assigned? Is it spelled correctly?


"18.5" + 2
TypeError
Are these types compatible with the operation?


float("missing")
ValueError
Is this text a valid representation of a number?


10 / 0
ZeroDivisionError
Can the denominator be zero?


if True without a colon
SyntaxError
Is the statement structurally valid?



A notebook remembers earlier executed assignments. If a result seems inconsistent, restart the kernel and run cells from the beginning. This revised chapter’s executable cells are designed to complete in order without interactive input or intentional infinite loops.
Debug: A measurement arrives as reading_text = "18.5". The expression reading_text + 0.5 fails. Explain the cause and repair it. Would the same repair work for the text "missing"?






NoteExplanation and repair





The expression mixes a string and a float. For numeric text, use float(reading_text) + 0.5, which gives 19.0. float("missing") raises ValueError; the program needs an explicit rule for missing text rather than assuming every string is numeric.

title: Python Basics
text:
Readiness Check
Try this task without looking at the solution. Use only ordinary Python.
For readings = [18.5, None, 21.0, 0.0, 105.0]:

Write a function that returns whether a reading is present and between 0 and 100 inclusive.
Use a loop to count and total valid readings.
Report their mean, or display "No valid readings" if the count is zero.
Explain why zero is included and None is excluded.
Repeat with [None, 105.0] to check the no-valid-data case.







NoteOne solution





def is_valid_reading(value, lower=0, upper=100):
    return value is not None and lower <= value <= upper

readings = [18.5, None, 21.0, 0.0, 105.0]
count = 0
total = 0.0
for value in readings:
    if is_valid_reading(value):
        count += 1
        total += value

if count > 0:
    print(f"Count: {count}; mean: {total / count:.2f}")
else:
    print("No valid readings")
The first list produces Count: 3; mean: 13.17. The second produces No valid readings. Zero meets the range rule; None represents an absent value and is checked before numerical comparisons.



Before moving on, confirm that you can:

Trace assignments and distinguish numerical values from text.
Write explicit conditions, including a check for None.
Choose a loop and explain when it stops.
Write and call a function that returns a reusable result.
Import a standard-library module and explain why importing is different from installing.
Distinguish an attribute from a method call.
Interpret an error message and check a notebook from a fresh session.

Next, review Data Structures, including sequences, mappings, iteration, and shared references. Then continue to Setting Up for Data Science.

title: Data Structures
text:
Check Your Starting Point
This chapter reviews how to organize, access, and transform data using the built-in Python structures covered in STAT 201. It builds on Python Basics. Use your existing Python setup; the executable examples need only Python and its standard library.
Our guiding question is: What information does this structure preserve, and what might an operation change or lose? This question matters when preparing data for exploration and analysis.
Predict the answers before running any code. Use the answers to decide which sections need your attention.

title: Data Structures
text:
What are values[-1] and values[1:3] for values = [10, 20, 30, 40]?
Would a list or a set preserve the order and repeated readings in [20, 20, 18]?
After a = [1, 2], b = a, and b.append(3), what is a?
What is result after values = [3, 1, 2] and result = values.sort()?
How many pairs does list(zip(["A", "B"], [10])) contain?
What is lost in dict([("A", 10), ("A", 20)])?







NoteAnswers and where to review






40 and [20, 30]. Review Accessing and Updating Values.
A list preserves both; a set removes duplicates and does not preserve first-occurrence order. Review Choosing a Data Structure.
[1, 2, 3], because both names refer to the same list. Review Shared References and Copying.
None; values itself becomes [1, 2, 3]. Review Sorting and Key Functions.
One pair: ("A", 10). Review Iteration and Unpacking.
The earlier value 10 for key "A" is overwritten. Review Working with Structured Records.

title: Data Structures
text:
Choosing a Data Structure
Choose a structure according to the operations and information you need, rather than memorizing syntax alone.











Structure
Order
Mutable?
Duplicates
Access
Typical use




list
Positional order
Yes
Allowed
Index or slice
A sequence of readings or records


tuple
Positional order
No
Allowed
Index or slice
A record with a fixed arrangement of fields


str
Character order
No
Allowed
Index or slice
Text


set
No guaranteed order
Yes
Removed
Membership; no indexing
Unique identifiers and overlap checks


dict
Insertion order
Yes
Keys unique; values may repeat
Key
Labeled fields or identifier-based lookup



A tuple’s immutability prevents replacing its elements; it does not make a nested mutable object immutable. Dictionary keys and set elements must be hashable. Strings and integers are common choices. A tuple is hashable only when all its elements are hashable: (101, "STAT303") works, but ([101], "STAT303") does not.

readings = [20, 20, 18]
station_location = (42.05, -87.68)
station_name = "North"
unique_readings = set(readings)
station = {"id": "N01", "name": station_name}
print(readings)
print(sorted(unique_readings))  # Sort for a predictable display, not arrival order.
print(station_location)
print(station)

[20, 20, 18]
[18, 20]
(42.05, -87.68)
{'id': 'N01', 'name': 'North'}


Choose and explain: Which structure would you use for an ordered measurement history, a collection of unique station IDs, and a station record with named fields?






NoteSuggested choices





Use a list for the history, a set for unique IDs, and a dictionary for named fields. Converting the history to a set would discard repeated measurements and their original order.

title: Data Structures
text:
Accessing and Updating Values

Indexing and Slicing
Sequence indexes start at zero; negative indexes count from the end. A slice excludes its stop position. Out-of-range indexing raises IndexError, whereas a slice can safely extend beyond the end.

values = [10, 20, 30, 40]
print(values[0])
print(values[-1])
print(values[1:3])
print(values[:2])
print(values[::2])
print(values[1:100])

10
40
[20, 30]
[10, 20]
[10, 30]
[20, 30, 40]




Updating Lists
append() adds one object. extend() adds each item from an iterable. These methods change the list in place and return None.

appended = [10, 20]
append_result = appended.append([30, 40])
extended = [10, 20]
extended.extend([30, 40])
print(appended)
print(extended)
print(append_result)
extended[0] = 11
print(extended)

[10, 20, [30, 40]]
[10, 20, 30, 40]
None
[11, 20, 30, 40]


Predict: What would extended.extend("50") add? Why is that different from extended.append("50")?






NoteAnswer





extend("50") adds two separate strings, "5" and "0", because a string is iterable. append("50") adds one string, "50". Neither operation converts text into a number.





Working with Text
String methods return new strings rather than changing the original string. strip() removes leading and trailing whitespace; split() separates text into pieces; a separator’s join() method joins an iterable of strings.

raw_label = "  north, temperature  "
parts = raw_label.strip().split(",")
clean_parts = []
for part in parts:
    clean_parts.append(part.strip())
print(raw_label)
print(clean_parts)
print(" | ".join(clean_parts))

  north, temperature  
['north', 'temperature']
north | temperature


split(",") is suitable for this simple label. CSV files can contain quoted commas and other rules, so use the standard-library csv module or a data-reading library for actual CSV data.


Dictionary Keys and Missing Values
record[key] retrieves a value or raises KeyError if the key is absent. record.get(key, default) returns the default for an absent key; without a supplied default it returns None. Membership in a dictionary tests keys, not values.

station = {"id": "N01", "reading": None}
station["unit"] = "C"
station["unit"] = "degrees C"  # Update the existing key.
print(station["id"])
print("reading" in station)
print("N01" in station)
print(station.get("reading", "not recorded"))
print(station.get("height", "not recorded"))

N01
True
False
None
not recorded


A present key whose value is None is different from an absent key. .get() does not replace an existing None with its default.


Sets and Membership
Use sets to find unique values and compare groups. Union finds values in either set; intersection finds shared values; difference finds values in one set but not the other.

expected_ids = {"N01", "S01", "E01"}
received_ids = {"N01", "S01", "W01"}
print("All IDs:", sorted(expected_ids | received_ids))
print("Shared IDs:", sorted(expected_ids & received_ids))
print("Missing IDs:", sorted(expected_ids - received_ids))
print("Unexpected IDs:", sorted(received_ids - expected_ids))

All IDs: ['E01', 'N01', 'S01', 'W01']
Shared IDs: ['N01', 'S01']
Missing IDs: ['E01']
Unexpected IDs: ['W01']


Dictionary key lookup and set membership are typically fast on average; list membership searches through values. Do not confuse membership with positional indexing: values[0] is direct list access, while sets do not support indexing. For this course, choose the correct representation before considering performance.

title: Data Structures
text:
Shared References and Copying
Assignment binds a name to an object; it does not automatically copy that object. Mutation changes an object. Rebinding changes which object a name refers to.

original_readings = [18.5, 21.0]
shared_readings = original_readings
shared_readings.append(0.0)
print(original_readings)
print(shared_readings is original_readings)
shared_readings = [99.0]
print(original_readings)
print(shared_readings)

[18.5, 21.0, 0.0]
True
[18.5, 21.0, 0.0]
[99.0]



Shallow Copies
list.copy() makes a new outer list. Appending to this copy does not change the original outer list, but objects nested inside both lists remain shared.

independent_readings = original_readings.copy()
independent_readings.append(30.0)
print(original_readings)
print(independent_readings)

nested = [[1], [2]]
shallow_copy = nested.copy()
shallow_copy[0].append(3)
print(nested)

[18.5, 21.0, 0.0]
[18.5, 21.0, 0.0, 30.0]
[[1, 3], [2]]


For nested structures, the standard-library copy.deepcopy() can recursively copy objects when independent nested data is required. Do not copy automatically: decide whether sharing is intended.


Function Arguments
A parameter refers to the object supplied by the caller. Mutating a passed list is visible to the caller; rebinding the parameter does not rebind the caller’s name. This behavior is often called call by sharing.

def append_zero(values):
    values.append(0.0)

def replace_locally(values):
    values = [99.0]
    return values

measurements = [18.5]
append_zero(measurements)
print(measurements)
print(replace_locally(measurements))
print(measurements)

[18.5, 0.0]
[99.0]
[18.5, 0.0]


Explain: When could an analysis be affected by appending to a list inside a function? How could you return an expanded list while preserving the caller’s list?






NoteOne solution





Later calculations may unexpectedly include the appended value. For a flat list, create a new list:
def with_zero(values):
    result = values.copy()
    result.append(0.0)
    return result

source = [18.5]
expanded = with_zero(source)
print(source)    # [18.5]
print(expanded)  # [18.5, 0.0]

title: Data Structures
text:
Iteration and Unpacking

Collections and Iterators
An iterable can supply an iterator to a loop. An iterator is also iterable: it remembers its position and becomes exhausted after producing its values. A list can supply fresh iterators for repeated passes; an already exhausted iterator does not restart itself.

readings = [18.5, 21.0]
reading_iterator = iter(readings)
print(next(reading_iterator))
print(list(reading_iterator))
print(list(reading_iterator))
print(list(readings))
print(iter(reading_iterator) is reading_iterator)

18.5
[21.0]
[]
[18.5, 21.0]
True


Calling next() on an exhausted iterator raises StopIteration; a for loop handles that signal automatically. next(iterator, default) can provide a fallback instead.


Unpacking and enumerate()
Unpacking assigns items to names. Ordinary unpacking needs the same number of names and items; starred unpacking collects remaining items into a list. enumerate() supplies a counter and an item. Its start argument changes the counter, not the underlying sequence indexes.

station_id, reading = ("N01", 18.5)
print(station_id, reading)
first, *rest = [10, 20, 30]
print(first, rest)
for row_number, label in enumerate(["North", "South"], start=1):
    print(row_number, label)

N01 18.5
10 [20, 30]
1 North
2 South


For dictionaries, use for key, value in record.items() when you need both labels and values.


Pairing with zip()
zip() returns an iterator of tuples paired by position. It does not match identifiers or verify that two inputs refer to the same entities. By default, it stops at the shortest input.

station_ids = ["N01", "S01", "E01"]
readings = [18.5, 21.0]
pairs = list(zip(station_ids, readings))
print(pairs)
print("Lengths match:", len(station_ids) == len(readings))

paired_ids, paired_readings = zip(*pairs)
print(paired_ids)             # A tuple, not a list.
print(list(paired_readings))  # Convert explicitly if a list is needed.

[('N01', 18.5), ('S01', 21.0)]
Lengths match: False
('N01', 'S01')
[18.5, 21.0]


Here E01 has no partner and is omitted. If equal-length lists are required, check their lengths before pairing. Python 3.10 and later also support zip(..., strict=True), which raises ValueError for mismatched lengths when consumed. Neither approach detects IDs in different orders. The unzip pattern above also assumes there are pairs to unpack.
Predict: Pair ["S01", "N01"] with [18.5, 21.0], assuming the readings originally belonged to North then South. Will zip() detect the mismatch?






NoteAnswer





No. It produces ("S01", 18.5) and ("N01", 21.0). Equal lengths do not establish correct alignment. Preserve IDs with their readings, or explicitly match records by ID.





Useful Functions and Their Limits








Tool
Purpose
Important detail




len()
Count items in a sized object
An arbitrary iterator may have no length


min(), max()
Find extrema
Empty input raises ValueError unless an appropriate default is supplied


sum()
Total numerical values
An empty input returns 0 with the default starting value


sorted()
Create a sorted list
Consumes an iterator supplied as input


reversed()
Iterate in reverse
Requires a reversible object; not every iterable supports it


all(), any()
Combine truth tests
all([]) is True; any([]) is False


separator.join()
Join text items
All items must be strings

title: Data Structures
text:
Comprehensions
Use a comprehension for a simple transformation or filter. Start with an ordinary loop, then compare the equivalent expression. Use a loop when several steps or branches make the comprehension difficult to read.

readings = [18.5, None, 21.0, -2.0, 0.0]
valid_readings = []
for value in readings:
    if value is not None and 0 <= value <= 100:
        valid_readings.append(value)

valid_comprehension = [
    value for value in readings
    if value is not None and 0 <= value <= 100
]
print(valid_readings)
print(valid_comprehension)

[18.5, 21.0, 0.0]
[18.5, 21.0, 0.0]


The expression comes first, then the iteration, then an optional filter. Square brackets build a list, braces around a single expression build a set, and braces around key: value build a dictionary.

squares = [number ** 2 for number in range(5, 9)]
labels = ["north", "south", "north"]
unique_labels = {label.upper() for label in labels}
label_lengths = {label: len(label) for label in labels}
print(squares)
print(sorted(unique_labels))
print(label_lengths)

[25, 36, 49, 64]
['NORTH', 'SOUTH']
{'north': 5, 'south': 5}


The set loses repetitions. The dictionary has only one value per key; repeated keys replace earlier values. Neither structure can preserve repeated records under the same key without additional design.
Write: From [" North ", "", "SOUTH", "   "], create a list of stripped, lowercase, nonempty labels.






NoteOne solution





raw_labels = [" North ", "", "SOUTH", "   "]
clean_labels = [label.strip().lower() for label in raw_labels if label.strip()]
print(clean_labels)  # ['north', 'south']

title: Data Structures
text:
Sorting and Key Functions

New List or In-Place Change?
sorted() returns a new list. A list’s .sort() changes that list and returns None. If you pass an iterator to sorted(), the iterator is consumed even though a new list is returned.

values = [3, 1, 2]
ordered = sorted(values)
print(values)
print(ordered)
result = values.sort()
print(values)
print(result)
print(sorted(values, reverse=True))

[3, 1, 2]
[1, 2, 3]
[1, 2, 3]
None
[3, 2, 1]




Choosing a Key
The key argument accepts a function that extracts each item’s sorting value. Pass the function itself; do not call it at the argument position. Equal keys retain their original relative order: Python sorting is stable.

words = ["pear", "apple", "banana", "kiwi"]
print(sorted(words, key=len))

def last_character(word):
    return word[-1]

print(sorted(words, key=last_character))
print(sorted(words, key=lambda word: word[-1]))

['pear', 'kiwi', 'apple', 'banana']
['banana', 'apple', 'kiwi', 'pear']
['banana', 'apple', 'kiwi', 'pear']


pear stays before kiwi when sorting by length because both have four letters and pear came first. The last-character example assumes nonempty strings.
A lambda creates a function from a single expression. It returns that expression’s value. Use it for a short key such as lambda record: record["reading"]; use def when a meaningful name or multiple steps improve clarity.

number_text = ["10", "2", "1"]
print(sorted(number_text))
print(sorted(number_text, key=int))

people = [("Chen", 22), ("Bob", 19), ("Ann", 22)]
print(sorted(people, key=lambda person: person[1]))
print(sorted(people, key=lambda person: (person[1], person[0])))

['1', '10', '2']
['1', '2', '10']
[('Bob', 19), ('Chen', 22), ('Ann', 22)]
[('Bob', 19), ('Ann', 22), ('Chen', 22)]


The first people sort preserves Chen-before-Ann for equal ages. The second explicitly breaks age ties alphabetically by name. Say which behavior you intend in a task.
Practice: Sort ["data", "python", "AI", "science"] alphabetically ignoring case. Then sort [-3, 1, -2, 5, 0] by absolute value, smallest first.






NoteSolutions





print(sorted(["data", "python", "AI", "science"], key=str.lower))
# ['AI', 'data', 'python', 'science']
print(sorted([-3, 1, -2, 5, 0], key=abs))
# [0, 1, -2, -3, 5]
Neither task needs a lambda because an existing function already supplies the desired key.









NoteOptional: map, filter, and reduce





map() transforms items and filter() selects items; both return iterators. A simple comprehension often expresses the same task more directly. functools.reduce() repeatedly combines values; prefer a clear built-in operation when one exists.
from functools import reduce
values = [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(list(map(lambda value: value ** 2, values)))
print([value ** 2 for value in values])
print(list(filter(lambda value: value % 2 == 0, values)))
print([value for value in values if value % 2 == 0])
print(reduce(lambda left, right: left * right, values))  # 24
Recognizing these tools is useful; mastering them is not a prerequisite for starting the data science libraries.

title: Data Structures
text:
Working with Structured Records
A list of dictionaries keeps each observation’s fields together and gives the fields names. Nested access combines sequence indexing with dictionary lookup.

records = [
    {"station": "N01", "reading": 18.5},
    {"station": "S01", "reading": 21.0},
    {"station": "N01", "reading": 19.0},
]
print(records[0]["reading"])
print([record["reading"] for record in records if record["station"] == "N01"])
print(sorted(records, key=lambda record: record["reading"]))

latest_by_station = {record["station"]: record["reading"] for record in records}
print(latest_by_station)

18.5
[18.5, 19.0]
[{'station': 'N01', 'reading': 18.5}, {'station': 'N01', 'reading': 19.0}, {'station': 'S01', 'reading': 21.0}]
{'N01': 19.0, 'S01': 21.0}


The dictionary retains only the last encountered reading per station, not every observation. Calling it “latest” is justified only if records are in time order. Here we know only their list order.

Preserve First-Occurrence Order
A set can track names already seen while a list preserves the desired output order.

names = ["Alice", "Bob", "Alice", "Charlie", "Bob", "Dave"]
seen = set()
unique_names = []
first_positions = []
for index, name in enumerate(names):
    if name not in seen:
        seen.add(name)
        unique_names.append(name)
        first_positions.append((index, len(name)))
print(unique_names)
print(sorted(first_positions, key=lambda pair: pair[1], reverse=True))

['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie', 'Dave']
[(3, 7), (0, 5), (5, 4), (1, 3)]


The positions refer to the original list, not positions after deduplication. For equal lengths, stable sorting preserves encounter order. In real data, identical names do not necessarily identify the same person; use a suitable identifier when available.

title: Data Structures
text:
Readiness Check
The following illustrative course-enrollment dataset has one tuple per enrollment:
(student_id, student_name, course_code, grade)
A student can appear in several courses. Repeated student IDs are therefore expected; they do not automatically indicate duplicate records. Keep the dataset below as the input for all tasks.

# Illustrative course-enrollment records (not real student data).
students = [
    (101, "Alice", "STAT303", 85),
    (102, "Bob", "STAT301", 92),
    (103, "Charlie", "STAT303", 78),
    (104, "Diana", "STAT301", 95),
    (105, "Eve", "STAT303", 88),
    (106, "Frank", "STAT304", 82),
    (107, "Grace", "STAT301", 90),
    (108, "Hank", "STAT304", 87),
    (109, "Ivy", "STAT303", 91),
    (101, "Alice", "STAT301", 88),
    (101, "Alice", "STAT304", 82),
    (101, "Alice", "STAT302", 86),
    (102, "Bob", "STAT303", 79),
    (102, "Bob", "STAT304", 85),
    (102, "Bob", "STAT302", 83),
    (103, "Charlie", "STAT301", 91),
    (103, "Charlie", "STAT304", 84),
    (103, "Charlie", "STAT302", 80),
    (104, "Diana", "STAT303", 89),
    (104, "Diana", "STAT304", 93),
    (104, "Diana", "STAT302", 96),
    (105, "Eve", "STAT301", 87),
    (105, "Eve", "STAT304", 90),
    (105, "Eve", "STAT302", 85),
    (106, "Frank", "STAT303", 76),
    (106, "Frank", "STAT301", 81),
    (106, "Frank", "STAT302", 79),
    (107, "Grace", "STAT303", 84),
    (107, "Grace", "STAT304", 88),
    (107, "Grace", "STAT302", 91),
    (108, "Hank", "STAT303", 80),
    (108, "Hank", "STAT301", 83),
    (108, "Hank", "STAT302", 82),
    (109, "Ivy", "STAT301", 94),
    (109, "Ivy", "STAT304", 89),
    (109, "Ivy", "STAT302", 92),
    (110, "Jack", "STAT303", 83),
    (110, "Jack", "STAT301", 86),
    (110, "Jack", "STAT304", 79),
    (110, "Jack", "STAT302", 81),
    (111, "Karen", "STAT303", 96),
    (111, "Karen", "STAT301", 92),
    (111, "Karen", "STAT304", 94),
    (111, "Karen", "STAT302", 98),
    (112, "Leo", "STAT303", 72),
    (112, "Leo", "STAT301", 75),
    (112, "Leo", "STAT304", 78),
    (112, "Leo", "STAT302", 74)
]

Work without the solutions first. Use only built-in structures and ordinary Python.

Identify the outer structure, each record’s structure, and the four field types.
Count enrollment records, unique student IDs, and unique course codes.
Find the minimum and maximum grades, and their numerical range (maximum - minimum).
Find the mean grade across enrollment records. Explain what each observation contributes.
Select STAT303 enrollments and sort by descending grade, breaking ties by ascending student ID.
Explain what would be lost by converting all records into a dictionary keyed only by student ID. Would (student_id, course_code) always be enough if students could retake courses?







NoteSolution: structure and counts





The outer structure is a list, each record is a tuple, and the fields have types int, str, str, and int.
student_ids = {student_id for student_id, name, course, grade in students}
course_codes = {course for student_id, name, course, grade in students}
print(len(students), len(student_ids), len(course_codes))
# 48 12 4
Sets are appropriate for counting unique identifiers, but not for preserving all enrollments.









NoteSolution: grade summaries





grades = [grade for student_id, name, course, grade in students]
if grades:
    low, high = min(grades), max(grades)
    print(low, high, high - low)
    print(sum(grades) / len(grades))
else:
    print("No enrollment grades")
The minimum is 72, the maximum is 98, the range is 26, and the enrollment-level mean is 85.6875. Each enrollment contributes one grade. If students had different enrollment counts, this would give more weight to students with more enrollments than a mean of student-level means would.









NoteSolution: filtering and sorting





stat303_records = [record for record in students if record[2] == "STAT303"]
ranked = sorted(stat303_records, key=lambda record: (-record[3], record[0]))
for student_id, name, course, grade in ranked:
    print(student_id, name, grade)
There are 12 STAT303 records. Karen (111) has the highest grade, 96; Leo (112) has the lowest, 72. Negating the grade sorts grades downward while the second key keeps student IDs ascending for ties.









NoteSolution: choosing a record key





Student ID alone repeats, so later records overwrite earlier records for the same student. A (student_id, course_code) key works for this dataset, but retakes would require another distinguishing field, such as term or attempt ID. Alternatively, a dictionary could map each student ID to a list of enrollment records.



Before moving on, confirm that you can:

Choose a structure based on order, duplicates, mutability, and access needs.
Retrieve and update values, including values inside nested records.
Distinguish mutation, rebinding, and shallow copying.
Unpack records and use enumerate() and zip() appropriately.
Explain iterator exhaustion and possible loss when pairing data.
Write a readable comprehension and a sorting key.
Distinguish enrollment counts from unique-student counts.
Explain what information a transformation keeps or discards.

title: 1  Jupyter Notebooks in VS Code
text:
1.1 Anaconda vs. VS Code
In STAT 201, you used Jupyter notebooks through Anaconda. Throughout STAT303, the Python sequence, you will consistently use VS Code to write and run .ipynb notebooks. In this sequence, you will also use Quarto to produce HTML assignment submissions.
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:
Anaconda and Visual Studio Code serve different roles and can be used together. Anaconda bundles Python, hundreds of packages, and environment-management tools, making it convenient but requiring more disk space. VS Code is a lightweight code editor that connects to your Python installation and lets you add extensions as needed. The table below compares their purposes and key features.
crumbs: 1  Jupyter Notebooks in VS Code

title: 1  Jupyter Notebooks in VS Code
text:
Anaconda
 Visual Studio Code (VS Code)




Overview
A Python distribution with environment-management tools
A powerful, flexible, and lightweight code editor


What it is
A distribution that includes Python, many common packages, and tools such as conda and Navigator
A free code editor from Microsoft, built on the open-source Code - OSS project


Main purpose
Makes it easy to install Python and manage packages and environments
Provides a modern, flexible environment to write, run, and debug code in Python and many other languages


Key features
• Preinstalls many popular data science packages• Environment management with conda• Anaconda Navigator graphical interface
• Clean, customizable interface• Python support through extensions• Integrated terminal and Jupyter notebook support through the Jupyter extension• Debugging, code navigation, and Git tools• Extensible through additional extensions• Works with different Python environments, including Anaconda environments





1.1.1 Why We Use VS Code Throughout STAT303
Throughout the STAT303 Python sequence, you will move from running individual code cells to managing complete analyses: reading data, writing and checking code, explaining results, and preparing reports. VS Code gives you one workspace for that process. Learning the workflow now lets you reuse it as the assignments become more complex.

Build on what you learned in STAT 201. You will still use Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files), with code cells, Markdown explanations, and outputs. VS Code becomes the place where you edit and run those notebooks, and it can connect to the Python installation you already have through Anaconda.
Keep each analysis organized. Opening a project folder puts your notebooks, datasets, and supporting files together in the Explorer. You can see which files belong to an assignment and practice using paths that work within that project.
Understand and troubleshoot your code. Code completion and function information help you work with unfamiliar libraries. Seeing code, outputs, and error messages together makes it easier to investigate a problem and check whether a change fixes it.
Use the same workflow for each submission. Run and check your notebook, save it, render it to HTML with Quarto from the integrated terminal, and inspect the report before submitting. Practicing these steps makes the submission process familiar across the sequence.

The tools have distinct jobs: VS Code is the workspace, the Python kernel runs your notebook code, and Quarto creates the HTML report. The notebook kernel and the terminal can use different Python environments; in this chapter and the next, you will learn how to check that each uses the environment you intend.






Figure 1.1: VS Code brings Python code, Jupyter notebooks, a kernel selector, and an integrated terminal into one workspace. The Python kernel runs in the background and remembers variables between cells.

text:
1.4 Select a Notebook Kernel and Run a Test Cell
Open activity01.ipynb, then use Select Kernel at the top right of the notebook to choose a working Python 3 environment. If the environment is not shown immediately, choose Select Another Kernel → Python Environments.






Figure 1.2: Choose a notebook kernel in VS Code by opening activity01.ipynb, selecting Select Kernel, and then choosing Python Environments.



For this chapter, choose the environment you used in STAT 201. If you used Anaconda’s default environment, choose base; it may be labeled conda or have anaconda3 or miniconda3 in its path. Your existing environment is sufficient for this first check. Chapter 2 guides you through creating a separate environment for this course. We recommend a recent Python 3 release, preferably Python 3.10 or newer, but the course does not require one exact version.
Run this in a notebook code cell, not the terminal:
import sys
print("Notebook is running")
print(sys.version)
print(sys.executable)
print(2 + 3)
You should see a Python version, the path to its executable, and 5. The executable path identifies the environment used by this notebook.
If your test cell runs successfully, continue to the next section. If Python or the notebook does not start, expand the troubleshooting guide below.






NoteIf Python or the Notebook Does Not Start





If no kernel appears, Python may still be installed; VS Code may not have found its environment.

No kernel is offered? Check that Microsoft’s Python and Jupyter extensions are enabled, restart VS Code, and open the kernel picker again. Choose Select Another Kernel → Python Environments if that option appears.
Previously used Anaconda? Open Anaconda Navigator and launch a local Jupyter notebook as you did in STAT 201. Run import sys followed by print(sys.executable). If it works, return to the VS Code kernel picker and look for an environment with the same path.
VS Code says ipykernel is required? Install it for the selected environment using the VS Code prompt. If that environment is managed or read-only, ask for assistance or follow Chapter 2 to create your own environment.
Still cannot find or run Python? Ask for setup assistance and share the error message. If no working installation is available, install a recent Python 3 release from the official Python website; Python 3.10 or newer is recommended.

text:
1.5 Code, Markdown, and Saved Outputs
Use code cells for computation and Markdown cells for explanations, headings, and answers. Run cells with their play controls or Shift+Enter. Save the notebook with Ctrl+S or Cmd+S.
A notebook remembers values from previously executed cells. Moving or editing a cell does not undo its earlier effects. Before considering work complete, restart the kernel, run all code cells in order, and save again. A successfully executed notebook should not depend on variables created in deleted cells.
The HTML submitted later will be generated from this saved notebook. Writing an explanation in a code comment is useful, but Markdown is better for the report’s narrative.
If your notebook is working, continue to the next section. If you encounter a problem, expand the troubleshooting guide below.






NoteNotebook troubleshooting












Symptom
First check




No kernel is offered
Python/Jupyter extensions are enabled; a Python interpreter is installed and discoverable


Code will not run
The cell is Code rather than Markdown and a kernel is selected


Output differs after restarting

You cannot find the data folder
The ZIP is extracted and the correct project folder is open

title: 1  Jupyter Notebooks in VS Code
text:
1.6 Render and Submit with Quarto
In STAT201, you already used Quarto to generate HTML from notebooks in your Anaconda-based workflow. The same Quarto application works with notebooks edited in VS Code. This is a refresher on completing that workflow in the new editor.

1.6.1 Check Your Existing Quarto Installation
Open Terminal → New Terminal in VS Code and enter:
quarto --version
A version number means this terminal can find Quarto. You do not need to reinstall it simply because you changed editors. If the command is not found, restart VS Code and check your existing Quarto installation. If it is missing, install the Quarto application from the official download page and open a new terminal.
The Quarto VS Code extension is optional for our workflow. It adds editing assistance and integrated previews; it is not required to run quarto render in the terminal. The Quarto application, the Python/Jupyter extensions used for notebooks, and the optional Quarto extension serve different purposes. See Quarto’s VS Code guide.


1.6.2 Keep the Template’s Report Settings
The practice notebooks start with a Raw cell containing settings like these:
---
title: "Activity 1: Your First VS Code Notebook"
author: "Your Name"
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
    toc: true
    code-fold: false
---
Edit the existing title and author when appropriate; retain the indentation and --- lines. This is YAML configuration, not Python code. Keep it in the supplied Raw cell. toc: true adds a table of contents, and code-fold: false keeps code visible for grading.
embed-resources: true puts ordinary figures and styling inside the HTML. It does not include your Python environment or input data for rerunning the work, and external websites or services can still require internet access.


1.6.3 Restart, Run All, Save, Render, Inspect
Quarto normally renders an .ipynb file using its saved outputs. It does not rerun notebook code by default. A successful render alone does not show that your current code runs correctly. Follow this sequence:

Select the intended notebook kernel. For Chapter 1, use your familiar working STAT201 environment; Chapter 2 introduces a project environment.
Restart the kernel and run every code cell from top to bottom. Resolve unexpected errors. Use Markdown headings and explanations near the results they discuss.
Save the notebook. Keep necessary imports and computations, and remove irrelevant exploratory output.
In the terminal, check that you are in the folder containing the notebook. List its files with ls on macOS, Get-ChildItem in Windows PowerShell, or dir in Windows Command Prompt. If needed, use cd with the actual folder path in quotes; Chapter 2 explains navigation in detail.
Run quarto render filename.ipynb --to html, replacing filename.ipynb with your notebook’s name. Quote a filename containing spaces, for example quarto render "my assignment.ipynb" --to html.
Open the resulting HTML in a browser. Check your name or required identifier, explanations, code, and current outputs. Copy only the HTML to another folder and open the copy to check that ordinary figures and formatting travel with it. Correct the notebook and repeat saving/rendering if anything is missing.

The standalone practice kits have no Quarto project configuration redirecting output, so the HTML is created beside the notebook. Keep the notebook and data for future work; upload the HTML requested in the activity or assignment. Detailed notebook rendering behavior is described in Quarto’s notebook guide.

title: 2  Project Environments, Packages, and File Paths
text:
2.1 What Is a Terminal?
In STAT 201, you may have used the terminal mainly to render a Quarto document as HTML. This chapter starts with what that terminal does and how to move between folders in it. You will then use it alongside VS Code notebooks to create a project Python environment, install packages, and locate a local data file.
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:
A terminal is a text interface where you type commands and read their output. Instead of clicking a folder or a button, you describe an action in text. A shell is the program that reads those commands and carries them out. Common shells include zsh or Bash on macOS, and PowerShell or Command Prompt on Windows.
If you typed a command such as quarto render assignment.ipynb --to html in STAT 201, you have already used a terminal: you asked the shell to start Quarto, gave it a notebook filename, and requested HTML output. You do not need to run this example now.
In VS Code, open Terminal → New Terminal. This integrated terminal lets you work beside your notebook without opening a separate application. Check its tab or dropdown for the shell name; this chapter provides separate commands where shells differ. See the VS Code terminal introduction for more about the interface.

title: 2  Project Environments, Packages, and File Paths
text:
Figure 2.1: The VS Code integrated terminal. This macOS example identifies the terminal prompt, uses the zsh shell, and shows the plus button for starting a new terminal.




2.1.1 Read the Prompt and Enter a Command
The prompt is the text that appears when the shell is ready for input. Yours might look like one of these examples:
student@laptop stat303-setup %
PS C:\Users\student\stat303-setup>
Type after the prompt and press Enter to run a command. Do not copy the prompt itself. Read any output, then wait for the prompt to return before entering the next command. Some successful commands produce no output.
A terminal can also run an interactive Python session. If you see >>>, Python is waiting for Python code; type exit() and press Enter to return to the shell before using the navigation commands below. In a notebook, Python code goes in a code cell and runs through the selected kernel.






Figure 2.2: Starting an interactive Python session in the VS Code terminal. Type python at the shell prompt and press Enter; the >>> prompt shows that Python is ready for Python code.

section: 2.2 Why Use the Terminal for Python Data Science?
text:
2.2 Why Use the Terminal for Python Data Science?
Your notebook holds calculations, plots, and explanations. The terminal helps you prepare and run the project around it:

Manage Python environments and packages. Create a separate environment for the project and install libraries such as Pandas into it.
Locate files. Check which folder you are working in and whether it contains the notebook or dataset a command needs.
Run project tools. Render an HTML report with Quarto or run a saved Python script.
Repeat a workflow. Save the commands you used so that you or a classmate can repeat the setup later.

For example, a data analysis assignment may involve installing Pandas in the terminal, analyzing a CSV in a notebook, and returning to the terminal to render the saved notebook as HTML. Keeping these steps in one VS Code workspace makes the workflow easier to follow.

title: 2  Project Environments, Packages, and File Paths
text:
2.3 Navigate in the Terminal
The terminal always has a current working directory, meaning the folder from which it interprets relative file and folder names. Here, directory and folder mean the same thing. Think of it as your current location in the folder tree: listing files shows what is here, and cd (change directory) moves you somewhere else.
With the extracted stat303-setup folder open in VS Code, open a terminal and select the tab matching your shell. Windows PowerShell and Windows Command Prompt are different shells. Run one command at a time.

macOS: zsh or BashWindows PowerShellWindows Command Prompt



Show the current directory: pwd
List files and folders: ls
Enter the data folder: cd data
Move to the parent folder: cd ..




Show the current directory: Get-Location
List files and folders: Get-ChildItem
Enter the data folder: cd data
Move to the parent folder: cd ..




Show the current directory: cd
List files and folders: dir
Enter the data folder: cd data
Move to the parent folder: cd ..




. means the current directory and .. its parent. A child folder is a folder directly inside the current one; the parent folder is the folder containing it. Put paths containing spaces in quotes, for example cd "course practice" when that folder exists inside your current directory. To change drives as well as folders in Command Prompt, use cd /d "D:\your\folder", replacing the example path with your actual path.

2.3.1 Try It: Visit the Data Folder and Come Back

Find your starting point. Show the current directory. It should be the extracted stat303-setup folder. If it is elsewhere, use cd with the actual path to your extracted folder, in quotes, then check again.
Look around. List its contents. You should see activity01.ipynb, activity02.ipynb, and data, among other files.
Enter the data folder. Run cd data, then show the current directory again. Its path should now end in stat303-setup/data (with backslashes on Windows).
Check what is inside. List the contents again. You should see station_readings.csv.
Return to the project folder. Run cd .., then show the current directory and list its contents. You should see the notebooks again.

These commands inspect folders and change the terminal’s location; they do not move your files. Navigation commands such as cd are shell commands and do not use Python, so you do not need to identify a Python environment before running them. If cd data reports that the folder does not exist, check your current directory and its contents before trying again. Clicking a file in Explorer does not change an existing terminal’s working directory, and cd in the terminal does not change a running notebook’s working directory.
Starting-folder check: finish in stat303-setup. This is where you will create the environment and write the requirements file later in this chapter.

title: 2  Project Environments, Packages, and File Paths
section: 2.4 Ask Three Questions Before a Command
text:
2.4 Ask Three Questions Before a Command
Throughout this course, you will use both notebooks and the terminal. Some tasks can be completed in either place, but the commands may differ. Your notebook and terminal may also use different Python environments or work from different folders.
Before running a command, ask these three questions to help avoid syntax errors, installing packages in the wrong environment, or failing to find files.








Question
In a notebook
In a terminal




1. Where am I typing?
Use a Python code cell for Python code.
Identify the shell; a >>> prompt means you are inside Python instead.


2. Which Python am I using?
Run import sys, then print(sys.executable).
Run python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)".


3. Which folder is current?
Run from pathlib import Path, then print(Path.cwd()).
Use pwd, Get-Location, or cd for your shell.



The terminal command python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)" starts Python, prints the executable path, and exits back to the shell. On macOS, use python3 instead if python is not available. Navigation commands such as cd do not use Python, so you do not need to check which Python environment is active before running them.
The notebook and terminal can use different Python installations and different working directories. Choosing a notebook kernel does not necessarily change which Python the terminal uses. Compare the two sys.executable outputs to identify which Python each uses; at this point, simply record what you find.
Similarly, the folder visible in Explorer does not prove either one’s current directory. Check the current directory in each place. A terminal command may find or create a file in one folder while the notebook looks for it in another.
Apply the check: identify where you are typing, record the Python executable used in each place, and confirm that the terminal’s current folder is stat303-setup. The next sections explain project environments and guide you through setting one up.
